turns.text: Hello, and welcome to the Wellbeing Podcast. I'm Nadia. Today we are talking about stress.
Think about the ten minutes before an exam. Your heart beats fast. Your hands are cold. You feel tense.
Many students feel like this. Some feel slightly uneasy. Some feel completely exhausted. Some are really irritable because they did not sleep, and they shout at their brother at home.
Here are six normal words for these feelings: anxious, frustrated, drained, restless, discouraged and overwhelmed. They are normal words. You are not broken.
Now, the interesting part. Scientists asked thousands of adults two questions. Question one: how much stress do you have? Question two: do you think stress is bad for you?

The people with a lot of stress who believed that stress was harmful had more health problems. But the people with a lot of stress who did not believe this were fairly healthy. In fact, they were very healthy.
So the belief is important. We call this your mindset.
Next time your heart beats fast, you can think: I am anxious, I cannot do this. Or you can think: this is energy, my body is helping me perform.
One more thing. When we have problems, we look for other people. We seek support. Asking for help is not weak.
So, you cannot always choose your stress. But you can choose the story you tell about it. See you next week.
Hello and welcome back to the Wellbeing Podcast. I'm Nadia, and today we're asking a simple question: is stress always the enemy?
Let's start with the words. When students describe a hard week, they usually say I'm stressed. But stressed is a very small word for a very big range of feelings.

You might be slightly uneasy before a presentation. You might be fairly anxious the night before a test. You might be rather irritable because of a bad night's sleep, or utterly exhausted after three exams in two days.
By Friday you might feel really drained and restless: too tired to work, too tense to relax. And if the marks don't improve, you feel discouraged, frustrated, and completely overwhelmed.
Emotions come in ladders. You can be annoyed, then angry, then furious. You can be tired, then worn out, then exhausted, then burnt out. Choosing the right rung is a skill.

Now, the research. In one famous study in the United States, scientists followed thousands of adults for eight years. They asked two questions: how much stress have you experienced this year, and do you believe that stress is harmful to your health?

Here is the surprise. People with high stress who believed stress was harmful had a much higher risk of serious health problems. But people with just as much stress who did not see it as harmful were among the healthiest people in the whole study.
So the stress itself was not the whole story. The belief mattered enormously. Psychologists call this your stress mindset.

Think about the signals. Your heart pounds before a presentation. You can read that signal in two ways. You can think: this is anxiety, I can't cope. Or you can think: this is energy, my body is preparing me to perform. As a result, students trained to read the second story felt more confident, and often performed better too.

And there's one more discovery. Stress doesn't only make us want to run away. It also pushes us to connect. Since we feel under pressure, we are more likely to seek support and to help others, and helping others actually protects our own health.

So the next time your heart races before an exam, try telling yourself a different story: this is my body helping me rise to the challenge. You cannot always choose your stress. But you can choose the story you tell about it.
Welcome back to the Wellbeing Podcast. I'm Nadia, and my guest today is Dr Amara Okonjo, who researches stress in adolescents. Dr Okonjo, students tell me they're stressed. Is that a useful word?

It's a useful starting point, but it's far too blunt. Compare three students. One is slightly uneasy before a presentation. One is rather apprehensive about a result that arrives on Friday. One is utterly exhausted after a fortnight of deadlines. Those are three different problems, and they need three different solutions.
So precision matters.

Precision is the whole intervention, in a sense. If a student can say I'm agitated rather than I'm fine, the conversation can begin. And notice the ladders. Annoyed, angry, furious, livid. Content, happy, delighted, over the moon. Down, sad, miserable, devastated. Each rung is a different level of intensity, and a fairly small vocabulary problem becomes a rather large emotional one.
Let's talk about the research that changed your field.

In one American study, researchers followed thousands of adults for eight years, asking two questions: how much stress have you experienced, and do you believe stress is harmful to your health? People with high stress who believed it was harmful had a substantially higher risk of serious illness. But people with just as much stress who did not see it as harmful were among the healthiest in the entire sample. Healthier, in fact, than people reporting very little stress.
That's counter-intuitive. So the stress wasn't the problem?

The stress was not the whole story. Due to the belief attached to it, the same physiology produced different outcomes. We call it a stress mindset. Your heart pounds before an exam. That signal is ambiguous. Read it as threat — I'm anxious, I can't cope — and you become tense, restless, completely drained and frequently discouraged. Read it as challenge — this is energy, my body is pumping oxygen to my brain so that I can perform — and confidence rises. Therefore performance often rises with it, because you are ready to rise to the challenge.
Is it really that simple? Just tell yourself a better story?

No, and I want to be careful here. Reframing does not repair a timetable with four assessments in one week. If a student is drained and frustrated because of genuine overload, the honest answer is that the load must change. Reframing helps you meet a challenge; it doesn't invent extra hours.
There's one more finding I loved.

Yes. Stress doesn't only trigger the impulse to escape. It also drives us towards other people. Since pressure makes us more likely to seek support — and, interestingly, to offer it — the social response protects our health. So when a student feels overwhelmed and irritable, the instinct to withdraw is exactly backwards. As a result, my advice is short. Name the feeling precisely. Read the signal as energy. And ask somebody for help before you are at breaking point.
Dr Okonjo, thank you. Next week: sleep, and why revising at two in the morning is so expensive that it costs you the exam.

Welcome back to the Wellbeing Podcast. My guest is Dr Amara Okonjo, who researches adolescent stress. Dr Okonjo, every wellbeing assembly I've ever sat through begins with the sentence stress is bad for you. Is it?

It's a serviceable slogan and a poor summary. Begin with the vocabulary, because the vocabulary is where the trouble starts. A student who is slightly uneasy before a seminar, one who is rather apprehensive about a result due on Friday, one who is completely exhausted after a fortnight of deadlines, and one who is utterly despondent after a term of near-misses are not experiencing the same condition. Collapse all four into stressed and you have guaranteed that nobody receives the right help.
So the imprecision is itself part of the harm.

It is. And notice how the ladders work. Annoyed, angry, furious, livid. Down, sad, miserable, devastated. Uneasy, worried, anxious, panicked. Each rung carries different information. There's a grammatical point buried in there, too: you can be fairly irritable, really tense or rather agitated, because those adjectives are gradable, but you cannot be slightly devastated. Devastated is a limit adjective. It has no dimmer switch.
Let's come to the study everyone quotes.

American researchers tracked thousands of adults across eight years, asking two things: how much stress have you experienced, and do you believe stress is harmful to your health? Those reporting high stress who also believed it was harmful showed a substantially elevated risk of serious illness. Those reporting equally high stress who did not regard it as harmful were among the healthiest in the sample — healthier, remarkably, than respondents reporting very little stress at all.
Which is the finding that launched a thousand assemblies.

And here I must be a spoilsport, because the study is observational, not experimental. Nobody assigned people to a belief. So the causal arrow may run backwards: people who are already healthy, well-supported and financially secure may find it considerably easier, because of those very circumstances, to regard stress as benign. Optimism, income and social support are all plausible confounders. And the measures are self-reported, which is to say approximate.
So should we stop telling students to reframe?

No — because the laboratory work is stronger than the survey. When you train participants to reinterpret a pounding heart — not as I can't cope, but as oxygen reaching the brain — you can measure the difference: they report greater confidence, their blood vessels behave differently, and they frequently perform better. They rise to the challenge. That's an experiment. What I object to is the leap from that finding to the claim that mindset is sufficient. If a fifteen-year-old is drained, restless, frustrated and discouraged, permanently on edge due to four assessments in one week, then the timetable is the pathology, and no amount of narrative repair will fix it. Therefore the honest formulation is: reframing helps you meet a challenge you have the resources to meet.
And the social finding?

That one I'd defend vigorously. Stress does not merely trigger flight; it drives affiliation. Since pressure makes us more inclined to seek support — and, crucially, to give it — the social response appears genuinely protective. Which makes the adolescent instinct to withdraw when overwhelmed almost perfectly counterproductive. As a result, my practical advice is unglamorous. Name the state precisely: apprehensive is not agitated, and neither is despondent. Read the signal as preparation rather than malfunction. And ask for help while you still have the capacity to describe what's wrong — not at breaking point, when you can't.
Dr Okonjo, thank you.
